newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: European dailies declare Kohl summit victor.
newsitem.headline: European dailies declare Kohl summit victor.

text.p: Leading European newspapers portrayed an EU summit deal on monetary union as a victory for German Chancellor Helmut Kohl with enough verbiage on unemployment to allow France to save face.

But some dailies said that European Union leaders had merely papered over a dispute about the controversial budget stability pact, and forecast that the compromise struck in Amsterdam on Monday would not hold.

Dailies across the EU said on Tuesday that the deal reached on the first day of the Amsterdam summit, which addressed French worries about high unemployment and German demands for a strong single European currency, allowed politicians on both sides of the dispute to look good.
But the compromise largely lacked substance, they said.

"(It) can be presented by both Bonn and Paris as a success," wrote the German daily Die Welt. "The euro will stay stable, (German) Finance Minister Theo Waigel will say, and his French counterpart will claim the stress on jobs as a victory in the fight against unemployment."
But Britain's Daily Telegraph echoed a belief among a number of leading dailies that Germany was the real winner at the two-day Amsterdam summit of EU leaders.
"It seems as though nothing can stop Chancellor Kohl from securing monetary union on his own terms," it said.
"All that the French Prime Minister Lionel Jospin has won is a banal statement to the effect that the EU recognises the importance of jobs," it said in an editorial.

Jospin's new Socialist-led government threw preparations for Amsterdam into confusion last week by saying the stability pact, which EU leaders agreed six months ago, had to address the problem of Europe's 18 million unemployed.
Germany refused to contemplate any changes to the pact, which commits countries joining the single European currency to running tight budgets, or extra spending to create jobs.
In the end France, which has one of the highest jobless rates in the EU, won a resolution expressing concern on unemployment but, the newspapers said, little else.
"With a weaker chancellor than Helmut Kohl the summit could have been very expensive for tax payers," wrote the German newspaper Bild, which is close to Kohl's government.
The London-based Financial Times also believed Germany came out better than the French Socialists, elected earlier this month on a promise to create jobs.
"A little thing like the French elections was never likely to shift the euro-train off its tracks," it said.
Some newspapers doubted the compromise marked anything more than a temporary truce in the dispute over jobs between France and Germany, the prime movers of European unity.

"There is no reason for celebration. The solution is just like most Brussels compromises: it is too thin to have any durability. It helps the French to save face at home," said Germany's Frankfurter Allgemeine. "But it will not be of much use either to them or their partners."
In Spain, which has the worst unemployment in the EU according to one measure, the mood was more positive.
"The accord yesterday was not a goal score, but the kickoff for a common fight against unemployment," said the leading daily El Pais.
But even French newspapers sympathetic to Jospin were lukewarm on the outcome in Amsterdam.
"A window was opened. Very good," the centre-left Liberation said. "(But) we are still far from the European growth pact envisioned by the Socialist Party congress."

The compromise included an EU jobs summit to be held in October. The Paris financial daily Les Echos said this would test whether the British, Germans and French could jointly commmit to anything more than vague objectives. "To tell the truth, there is little chance," it said.
